Gordon's play remains an impeccable piece of writing.
Director Amit Sharma controls the mood deftly, giving each scene just enough time to breathe without losing momentum, making sure every jabbing punchline lands and every hurtful truth hits home.
Amit Sharma’s production often careers along like an unabashed sitcom.

Dealing with the issues of Windrush and diaspora, punctuated by bursts of catchy calypso and reggae (sound design by Mwen), Nine Night is a generously warm-hearted and moving rendering of family grief and estrangement.
This revival by the Kiln’s artistic director Amit Sharma is perhaps a step towards cementing it as a classic for which productions can – and should – come about quite regularly.
Nine Night has stood the test of time and remains one of the most thoughtful explorations of Jamaican tradition and culture that has ever been written.
Director Amit Sharma’s successful revival celebrates the pain and messiness of family funerals, with much humour and some moments that catch your breath.
A fascinating if fraught family drama.
Natasha Gordon’s Nine Night earns the title of modern classic, and Amit Sharma’s production should help to cement that legacy.
Nine Night is a generously warm-hearted and moving rendering of family grief and estrangement.
Gordon’s warmly felt comedy-drama skilfully balances heartache with humour.
Long after the laughter fades, it’s Lorraine who stays with you.
In this production, everything seems amplified: the humour is sharper and quicker, the conflicts are more intense and constantly on the verge of eruption, and the grief is even more overwhelming.
We leave the theatre feeling as if we have met a group of people we would like to know better, but to whom we have only been briefly introduced.
Nine Night is funny, moving, gloriously unfiltered and full of heart.
It is a picture of joy that reminds us that everything we do matters, and that it will live on long after we’ve gone: in our memories, and in the people who carry them forward.

Nonetheless, this remains a deeply felt and funny assessment of familial grief, grounded by a lead performance that captures all of the contradictory emotions brought about by the loss of a difficult parent.
Nine Night has the bones of a truly great play, and its Kiln iteration is certainly worth a visit.
It’s a promising draft — but a draft, nonetheless.

cn.t: Critics widely embrace this Kiln Theatre revival of Natasha Gordon's modern classic, praising its warmth, humor, and emotional depth. Llewella Gideon's scene-stealing turn as Auntie Maggie earns particular acclaim.
